Fantastic to see new research from @verityharding's project @AIxGEO at the University of Cambridge which challenges how we usually talk about the AI supply chain. The paper maps the AI supply chain in detail - across 14 layers and 137 elements - analysing what areas are currently overlooked by policymakers, along with countries’ supply chain strengths and dependencies. It emphasises that no single country - not even the US and China together - can control the entire AI supply chain alone, with even well-known chokepoints depending on the assets and expertise of several countries at once. For European countries, it shows that far from being passive recipients of AI from other places they actually control more elements of the supply chain than they might have thought. It also finds that, across the policy documents analysed, over a third of the chain isn't mentioned at all. So many countries are overlooking their own strengths and ways in which they can bolster their position in the AI economy. Read more here: https://www.bennettschool.cam.ac.uk/publications/the-invisible-ai-supply-chain/

Another very interesting paper from Google on self-improving agent harnesses. (bookmark it) They let an optimizer rewrite the harness around a frozen Gemini 3.8 Flash on SWE-bench Lite and compared three approaches. - A prompt rule file lowered held-out accuracy from 5.0% to 2.5%. - A full rewrite of the harness reached 42.5% at 451.6k tokens per task. - Gated edits to one module at a time reached 40.0% at 46.7k tokens per task. The gated version splits the harness into four parts (context, control, tools, and verification). Each round it patches one part, checks the patch on held-out tasks under a token cap, and deploys it only if it passes. The gated harness also transferred to Gemini 4 Argon with no new search, solving 37.5% against 30.0% for the full rewrite. The test set is small (40 held-out issues), so treat the numbers as directional. The paper also lists failure modes to guard against when a harness edits itself, including prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22299 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/harnesses-that-improve-themselves-a-unifying-framework-for-self-improving-agent-2611.22299

Really good work from OpenAI researchers and colleagues. They trained a model to write its reasoning in different personas, and they noticed that chain-of-thought monitors started missing its hidden side tasks. On covert side-task evaluations, the monitorability score of a gpt-oss-20b model organism fell from 0.94 to 0.68 with no instruction to hide anything. The training data had no examples of evading a monitor. It only taught the model to control the style of its reasoning, and that control carried over to hiding. When the model was told to hide its side task, the score dropped to 0.22, and in some evaluations, close to zero. The effect also appeared in a Kimi-K2.6 model in agentic environments. Side tasks that needed long reasoning or many steps stayed easier to catch. Targeted prompts asking the model to reason transparently recovered much of the lost monitorability, sometimes above the base model. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21799 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/chain-of-thought-controllability-can-reduce-chain-of-thought-monitorability-2611.21799

// RAG in a Trenchcoat // This NeurIPS 2026 paper shows that a minimal RAG memory matches state-of-the-art agent memory systems on standard benchmarks. (bookmark it) BRIDGE stores chained observation notes, retrieves them with BM25 plus embeddings, and shows them in time order. It uses one LLM call per write or query and about 5-7K tokens per question. It matches the prior best within confidence intervals on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points. The authors then test what memory lets an agent do. In their probes, the agent must apply a remembered rule or pattern that the question never mentions. No single design wins all probes. LangMem, which extracts atomic facts, wins rule application. BRIDGE wins pattern induction. Fact extraction loses the shape of a demonstrated pattern, while block summaries retrieve the rule, but the agent often does not apply it. Showing the rule more prominently closes most of that gap. Don't overcomplicate your memory system. Old retrieval methods are still very useful for agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22179 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/rag-in-a-trenchcoat-when-minimal-memory-is-enough-for-agentic-systems-and-when-i-2611.22179

Do LLM agents still need to be told how to self-improve? A new paper from MIT CSAIL and the University of Tübingen tests this directly. They give a frozen model a compute budget and simple tools. It can write practice games, watch another copy of itself play them, and edit that copy's prompt and skill files. It does not see real tasks or validation scores, and it is not told how to learn. Capable models built a working learning procedure on their own and improved on held-out games with hidden mechanics. Models from different families arrived at similar strategies. They wrote games at a calibrated difficulty, ran controlled A/B comparisons, built their own validation suites, and spent more effort on harder tasks. The text files they produced also improved play on external benchmarks with different horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation. This matters for safety as well. Leaving out an explicit self-improvement loop does not stop a capable model from improving itself when it has the tools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23219 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/do-llm-agents-still-need-to-be-told-how-to-self-improve-2611.23219
